Physical UI

Three ordinary forms on three materials. Grab one by its background and pull it about, then let go. Press a button or type and the material takes the hit. Scroll the page and they lag behind. Through all of it the fields keep focus, the caret keeps blinking and clicks land on what you see.

Jelly

A soft body. It wobbles and springs back.

 <physical-ui material="jelly">

Cloth

Hung from a rail along its top edge. It swings like a pendulum and catches the wind.
<physical-ui material="cloth" wind="0.12">

Paper

Taped at the top corners. Stiff: it bends and lifts rather than stretching.

 <physical-ui material="paper">
Show the code forms on jelly and cloth
  1. Wrap a form in <physical-ui material="…">. The form is ordinary HTML and keeps working.
  2. Load the element. Wind and gusts are optional. all is the three elements.
  3. Inside the element: the form becomes a texture that is drawn on a simulated mesh. This is the WebGL route; on WebGPU the call is device.queue.drawElementImageToTexture({ source }, { texture }).
  4. Inside the element: hit testing follows the mesh. Find the triangle under the pointer, work out the affine matrix that carries its flat shape to its bent shape, and hand that to updateElementGeometry(). A click then lands on the control you see.
  5. The whole element.
<script type="module" src="/lib/physical-ui.js"></script>

<physical-ui material="cloth" wind="0.1">
  <form>…a real form…</form>
</physical-ui>

How it works

  • The form is a texture on a mesh. texElementSubImage2D() uploads the element whenever it repaints (typing, focus rings, the caret). The mesh is a grid of point masses joined by distance constraints, stepped with Verlet integration and lit from its surface normals.
  • WebGPU first, WebGL behind it. The mesh shader is written in both WGSL and GLSL. The element uses WebGPU when the browser has a real adapter that passes a self-test and accepts the first frame, and WebGL otherwise; the line under the wind control says which and why, and backend="webgpu|webgl" names one by hand. The simulation and hit testing are the same code either way.
  • Materials are parameters. Jelly has soft links and a spring to home. Cloth has stiff links, a pinned top edge and a pendulum-like pull home that weakens down the sheet. Paper adds bending links so it folds instead of stretching.
  • Hit testing uses the triangle under the pointer. An element only has one transform, and a wobbling mesh is not one transform. But only the point under the cursor matters, so each frame the element's geometry is set to the affine transform of the mesh triangle the pointer is over. The control you see under the cursor is the one you click.
  • At rest it is exactly the layout box, and the simulation stops. Nothing runs until you touch it. With reduced motion on, it never moves.
  • Keyboard and assistive tech see a normal form. Tab order, labels and focus are untouched; activating a control from the keyboard still pokes the material.
